body: I’ve seen UI patterns in which there is overscroll in multiple directions. The `toggle-overscroll` command seems limiting in that regard, as one would need to indicate which edge they want to overscroll. Maybe we need multiple commands? Or a way to pass some extra data to a command (e.g. `[commanddata]`)?

When you say that there is overscroll in multiple directions, do you mean that it's the same element that can be overscrolled in multiple direction or that there is two different elements that overscroll in two different directions? The latter is supported with toggle-overscroll, since you need to have two elements with `command="toggle-overscroll"`, each pointing to a different element in their `commandfor` attribute. In this case it is unambiguous which command toggles which overscroll.

In the former case, I agree that this isn't solved by the proposal. I'm supportive of exploring something like `commanddata` for additional information. For the command name, I prefer a simple command that does the right thing for the common case
I mean the former indeed. The Gmail app for example has this, in which overscrolling to the left or right reveal two different actions.

Heh, I see where the confusion comes from. In this sentence … > it's the same element that can be overscrolled in multiple direction … I interpret “the element” as being the scroll container, not the element that is in an overscroll area: you can overscroll the scroll container in two directions (with each direction revealing something else). > This set up would necessitate two buttons, avoiding ambiguity. In my POV in which I am looking at this as “the scroll container” instead of “the element in the overscroll area”, then the `toggle-overscroll` action should be directed at the scroller instead of the contents you want to reveal. That’s what lead to me suggesting an extra piece of necessary data to go along with `toggle-overscroll`. Looking at the explainer and the code, I see the command is directed at (the element placed inside) the overscroll area. In that sense, the action is more something like a `scrollIntoView`, no? > [piece of code] Looking at the code, putting the buttons inside the overscroll area feels very weird: - I would assume that content shown in an overscroll area is inerted until that area is revealed, so those buttons can never be reached, right? - Calling `e.preventDefault()` to change the behavior of the button when it’s activated is just nasty. The button that archives the email should not be the same button as the one that enables overscroll. This leads me to believe that the button that controls overscroll (*) is separate from the buttons with the interface actions ```html
from: vmpstr to: bramus
``` Activating the command buttons would make the relevant overscroll region visible (and focus its first focusable element), cfr. opening a dialog.

The CSS Working Group just discussed `Overscroll areas via command=toggle-overscroll`.
